cues.text: Eleven.
Final consolidation.
We now bring together the main ideas of this session, and the whole chapter rests on one principle: technical delivery and human adoption must work together.
A system can be built on time, on budget and to specification, and still fail if people do not use it, trust it, or change how they work because of it.
Equally, people can be fully willing and still be let down by technology that does not work.
Digital transformation needs both.
The source asks you to master twelve things.
Let us take them in order.
First, Kotter.
John Kotter's model treats change as a sequence of eight steps.
You create a sense of urgency.
You build a guiding coalition of influential people.
You form a strategic vision.
You enlist a volunteer army, meaning a wide group of people who want to take part.
You enable action by removing barriers.
You generate short-term wins.
You sustain acceleration, so early success does not lead to complacency.
And you institute change, anchoring the new ways of working in the culture.
The logic is that large change fails when people do not feel it matters, when leaders are not united, or when the change fades before it becomes habit.
Second, Lewin.
Kurt Lewin offers a simpler three-stage view: unfreeze, change, and refreeze.
Unfreezing means helping people see why the current way of working is no longer enough.
Change is the movement to the new state.
Refreezing means stabilising the new state so that people do not slide back to old habits.
Notice how Lewin and Kotter overlap.
Kotter's urgency belongs to unfreezing, and his anchoring belongs to refreezing.
Third, ADKAR.
Where Kotter and Lewin describe the organisation's journey, ADKAR describes the individual's.
The letters stand for Awareness of why change is needed, Desire to take part in it, Knowledge of how to change, Ability to put that knowledge into practice, and Reinforcement to make the change last.
The key idea is that these come in order.
If someone lacks desire, extra training in knowledge will not help.
ADKAR therefore helps you diagnose where a person or team is stuck.
Fourth, the causes of resistance.
Resistance is not just stubbornness.

Consider why people resist: they may not understand the reason for change, they may fear losing status, skills or jobs, they may lack the training, or they may simply distrust how the change is being handled.
Each cause points to a different response, and this is where ADKAR becomes practical.
Treat the cause, not the symptom.
Fifth, stakeholder engagement.
Stakeholders are the people and groups affected by a change or able to influence it.
Engagement means identifying them, understanding their concerns and interests, communicating with them, and involving them early rather than informing them after decisions are made.
People support what they have helped shape.
Now we turn from managing change to the customer side of the chapter.
Sixth, CX versus UX.

Customer experience, or CX, is the whole of a customer's perception and interaction with an organisation across every touchpoint and over time: discovering, buying, using, getting support, and returning.
User experience, or UX, is narrower.
It concerns how easy and satisfying it is to use a specific product, app or interface.
So UX is a part of CX.
A beautifully designed app, which is good UX, can sit inside a poor CX if delivery is late or support is unhelpful.
Seventh, journey mapping.
A customer journey map lays out, step by step, what a customer does, thinks and feels as they move through their interaction with you, from first awareness to after-sale.
Its value is that it reveals pain points, gaps and moments that matter, often exposing problems between departments that no single team can see.
Eighth, omnichannel.
Omnichannel means that the customer's various channels, such as website, mobile app, phone, social media and physical locations, are connected into one consistent experience.
This is different from simply being present on many channels.
In a true omnichannel approach, a customer can start in one channel and continue in another without repeating themselves.
Ninth, personalisation.
This means tailoring interactions, offers or content to the individual, using what you know about them, such as their history, preferences and behaviour.
It depends on good data, and it should be done in a way that customers find helpful rather than intrusive.
Tenth, CRM, or customer relationship management.
CRM refers to the strategy, practices and systems an organisation uses to record and manage customer interactions and data.
It is the foundation that makes omnichannel consistency and personalisation possible, because every team can work from the same view of the customer.
Eleventh, experience measures.
If you want to improve the customer experience, you must measure it.

The source asks you to know these measures, because what is not measured is difficult to manage, and because measures show whether a change is actually improving the experience rather than merely being delivered.
Twelfth, the AgriTech case.
The source lists this case for revision, and it is where the two sides of the chapter meet.
This block does not give the case details, so I will not add any.
When you revisit the case in your materials, read it through the principle we started with.
Ask what the technical delivery was, and ask what human adoption required: who had to change, who had to be engaged, what resistance might arise, and how the customer's experience would be affected.
Then ask whether both worked together.
To close, hold these in two groups.
Kotter, Lewin, ADKAR, resistance and stakeholder engagement help you bring people through change.
CX, UX, journey mapping, omnichannel, personalisation, CRM and experience measures help you design and check what customers actually experience.

The AgriTech case tests both together, and the lesson is the same throughout: technology delivered without adoption does not transform anything, and adoption without working technology has nothing to adopt.
